title: Retention skeleton: hook, lock-in, best points first, re-hook, then the rest and one aligned CTA
when: When a script explains a set of points, lessons, reasons, steps or stories (list-shaped videos, long or short).
summary: Order the script so the viewer has a reason to stay at every turn: a hook, a lock-in stretch that tells them exactly what they will get and why it matters to them, the two strongest points, a re-hook that reopens curiosity, the remaining points (optional fifth and sixth only if they earn their place), an optional short closing, and one call to action that matches the video's goal and offers something that fits what they just watched.
steps: Hook: one line that opens a specific curiosity gap or tension.
Lock-in zone: say what the viewer will walk away with and why it matters to them now; no channel intro.
Point 1 and point 2: the strongest material.
Re-hook: a sentence that reopens curiosity about what is still coming.
Points 3 and 4, then points 5 and 6 only when they are as strong.
Optional closing that pays off the hook.
One call to action aligned with the goal, with a matching next step (a related video, a free resource).
do: Keep the order visible in an outline before writing the full script.
avoid: A channel intro or greeting before the hook.
Saving the best point for the end.
checks: The first two points are the strongest in the outline.
There is a re-hook between point 2 and point 3.
There is exactly one call to action.
source: Kallaway Marketing script-structure carousel (Instagram, 2026-10-06), shared by the owner as a screenshot on 2026-10-21; restated

title: At least three points, never more than six
when: When a script is built from separate points, lessons, reasons or steps.
summary: Fewer than three points feels thin; more than six blurs together and loses viewers in the middle. If research gives more, merge related ones or keep the extra for another video.
avoid: Padding a thin topic to reach three points.
Listing seven or more points in one video.
checks: The point count is between 3 and 6.
source: Kallaway Marketing script-structure carousel, rules slide (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Put the best material in the first two points
when: When ordering the points or beats of any script.
summary: Most viewers decide in the first minutes whether the video keeps its promise. Spend the strongest examples, the most surprising fact and the clearest pay-off early, so the viewers who would leave see the best of the video first.
avoid: Building slowly toward the best point at the end.
checks: Point 1 or point 2 carries the most surprising or useful material.
source: Kallaway Marketing script-structure carousel, rules slide (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Re-hook after the second point
when: When a script has three or more points or beats, at the point where attention usually dips.
summary: After the second point, add one or two sentences that reopen curiosity: tease what is coming, raise the stakes, or flag that the next part changes the picture. It recaptures viewers who are drifting.
steps: Name what is still ahead without giving it away.
Tie it back to what the viewer wants from the video.
avoid: A generic 'stay tuned' or 'keep watching'.
A re-hook that promises something the video never delivers.
checks: The sentence after point 2 opens a new question or raises the stakes.
source: Kallaway Marketing script-structure carousel, rules slide (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Each point: name it, then one or two sentences on why it serves the video's promise
when: When writing each point, lesson or step of a list-shaped script.
summary: State the point plainly, then add one or two sentences that tie it back to the original objective (what the viewer came for). This keeps every section feeling relevant, so viewers do not feel the video wandering.
steps: Name the point in one sentence.
Explain in one or two sentences how it moves the viewer toward the promised result.
Then give the example, story or proof.
checks: Every point says how it connects to the promise of the title and hook.
source: Kallaway Marketing script-structure carousel, list-point slide (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Cold open: a specific curiosity gap in the first 15 seconds, then the promise
when: When writing the first 15 seconds of a long-form video.
summary: Start inside the story or the problem, with no channel intro or greeting. Open one specific question the viewer wants answered (a person, a number, a strange result), then promise what they will know by the end. A vague gap ('you won't believe this') does not hold anyone.
steps: Open on a concrete moment, claim or question.
Make the gap specific: who, what number, what happened.
State the promise: what the viewer will know or be able to do by the end.
avoid: Welcome, hi guys, my name is, in this video.
Asking for a subscribe before giving anything.
A vague tease without a concrete detail.
checks: No greeting or channel intro in the first 15 seconds.
The first minute states what the viewer will get by the end.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 3 'retention-first script structure' (shared by aiautomationchannels on Instagram; owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Three to five escalating beats, each ending on a small cliffhanger
when: When a long-form script tells a story or builds an argument rather than listing points.
summary: Break the middle into 3-5 beats or reveals that get bigger as the video goes on. End each beat with a pull forward: an unanswered question, a twist, or a hint of what the next reveal changes. Tension between reveals is what stops drop-off.
steps: Outline the reveals from smallest to biggest.
Write each beat so its last line points to the next one.
Let the biggest reveal answer the hook.
avoid: Beats that end on a full stop with nothing left to wonder about.
Revealing the biggest answer before the middle.
checks: Most beats end with a question, a turn or a forward hint.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 3 'retention-first script structure' (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: The payoff answers the hook
when: When writing the ending of any script.
summary: The last section must answer the exact question or tension the hook opened, using the same people, numbers or images. An ending that drifts to a new topic makes the viewer feel tricked and hurts the next click.
checks: The ending names the same subject the hook opened and resolves it.
avoid: Ending on a generic summary that never returns to the hook.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 3 'retention-first script structure' (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Specific numbers, names and stakes instead of vague claims
when: Whenever a script makes a claim, sets up a story or describes a result.
summary: Concrete details (a year, an amount, a named person or place, what was at stake) make a claim believable and keep attention; vague words (amazing, huge, many people) lose it. Use only details the evidence supports.
do: Replace 'a long time ago' with the year, 'a lot of money' with the amount, 'a famous general' with the name.
avoid: Inventing numbers or names to sound specific.
checks: Each section has at least one concrete number, name or stake.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 4 'script performance breakdown' (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Short-form frame: hook, value, solution, one call to action
when: When writing a Short or any video under a minute, or a self-improvement explainer that solves one problem.
summary: Hook: grab attention at once. Value: explain the problem, mistake, misconception or insight so the viewer feels understood, with useful information and no filler. Solution: a clear, actionable answer, using steps, a framework or examples when it helps. Call to action: one next step that matches the video's goal.
steps: Hook in the first line.
Value: name the problem or misconception and why it matters to the viewer.
Solution: the clear answer, as steps or an example.
One call to action matched to the goal.
avoid: Filler between the hook and the value.
A solution that is only a slogan.
checks: The viewer could act on the solution today.
source: HOOK / VALUE / SOLUTION / CTA reel framework posted by aashrayy0 and aikathekedaar (Instagram; owner screenshots 2026-10-21); restated

title: One call to action, matched to the video's goal
when: When ending a script or choosing what to ask the viewer to do.
summary: Ask for one thing only, and pick it from the video's goal. For followers, give a real reason to follow (what they will keep getting). For comments, ask an easy but meaningful question. For saves, make the content worth coming back to. For shares, name who should receive it. For leads or sales, offer a natural next step without sounding desperate. On YouTube the strongest default is the next video that continues the same promise.
avoid: Asking to like, subscribe, comment and share all at once.
A call to action before the viewer has received any value.
checks: The script contains exactly one call to action, placed after the payoff.
source: HOOK / VALUE / SOLUTION / CTA reel framework (aashrayy0, aikathekedaar; owner screenshots 2026-10-21) and Kallaway's 'CTA with an aligned lead magnet'; restated

title: Break down a script that held viewers: hook, re-hooks, tension, specificity, ending
when: When studying a script or transcript of a video that performed well on watch time (ours or a competitor's), to learn techniques for future scripts.
summary: Look at five things: what the first 15 seconds do; where re-hooks or pattern interrupts fight drop-off; how tension is built between reveals; how specifics (numbers, names, stakes) replace vague claims; and how the ending drives the next click or a subscribe. Record techniques in your own words, never the wording.
steps: Mark the hook and what gap it opens.
Mark each re-hook and pattern interrupt with its time.
Note how each reveal sets up the next.
List the concrete details used.
Note how the ending hands off to the next video.
avoid: Copying phrases from the studied script (the 8-word copy guard applies).
checks: Every finding names a technique, not a sentence to reuse.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 4 'script performance breakdown' (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Underserved niche test: demand and watch-time potential, but few doing it well
when: When proposing or judging a niche for a faceless long-form channel.
summary: A good niche has real search demand and topics people will watch for 8-15 minutes, but few channels doing it well. For each candidate, name the core audience, why they would watch a full video instead of scrolling past, three example titles with strong click potential, and the closest existing channel doing something similar.
steps: Show the demand (searches, rising channels, trend videos).
Say why a viewer would finish a full video.
Write three example titles.
Name the closest existing channel and what it does badly.
avoid: Calling a niche underserved without naming the closest competitor.
checks: The closest competitor is named and its weakness is concrete.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 1 'niche and format finder' (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Topic ideas: a curiosity title under 60 characters, the core promise, and why click this over the competitor
when: When proposing video topics or titles for search and suggested video.
summary: Each idea carries three parts: a curiosity-driven title under 60 characters, the core promise the video delivers, and the reason someone would click it over a similar video from a competing channel. If the third part is empty, the idea is a copy.
avoid: Titles longer than 60 characters.
A promise the script cannot keep.
checks: Every idea states why it beats the similar competing video.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 2 'topic and title research' (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Revenue paths beyond AdSense that fit this exact audience
when: When judging a niche or planning a channel's business model.
summary: List realistic revenue paths that fit the content naturally: sponsor categories this audience trusts, a digital or info product they would actually buy, and recurring formats (a series, a deep-dive playlist) that raise session watch time and channel loyalty. For each, say why it fits this audience rather than being a generic YouTube play.
avoid: Generic advice that would fit any channel.
checks: Each path names why this audience in particular would pay or watch more.
source: Paul Hilse, prompt 5 'monetization and offer ideas' (owner screenshot 2026-10-21); restated

title: Model the viewer before writing: who, wants, pains, why they stay, why they leave
when: Before judging a niche, choosing topics or writing a script for a family.
summary: Write down who watches (one sentence), what they want from this kind of video, the pains that bring them, what keeps them watching to the end, and what makes them click away. Use it to choose the hook, the order of points and the examples, and to cut anything that triggers a reason to leave.
steps: One sentence on who watches.
Up to five wants and five pains.
Up to five reasons they stay to the end.
Up to five reasons they leave.
Check the script against the reasons they leave.
checks: The script avoids every listed reason viewers leave.
source: Owner request 2026-10-21 ('what audience and viewers love to watch, how to make them sit and watch') with the core-audience question from Paul Hilse's prompt 1; restated
